title: How Dickhead Decisions Turn Ordinary People into Dicks
author: Richard Claydon
summary: In the second of a three-part series on workplace pathologies, Richard Claydon traces how a single flawed decision (a growth target, transformation programme, or strategic slogan) becomes an organizational pathology that turns ordinary, decent employees into what he calls 'dicks.' His mechanism has three stages: first, a 'dickhead decision' meets contradicting reality and, instead of being revised, gets protected by escalating authority (what he calls the shift from 'stern ruler to foolish paternalist' — confidence outliving understanding); second, the decision becomes a moral test, where questioning it starts to look like disloyalty rather than accuracy, so 'evidence has quietly become morality'; and third, fear transmits the resulting pressure down the hierarchy until it surfaces as human harm — humiliation, impossible targets, and self-betrayal at the frontline. Claydon's sharpest observation is that people rarely experience themselves as behaving badly while this happens: organizational pressure relabels aggression as decisiveness and manipulation as getting things done, so ordinary people stay dickish while believing themselves reasonable. He closes with a pointed critique of corporate resilience training, arguing it often just makes a broken system more durable by relocating the problem onto the individual, and proposes a different diagnostic question for leaders: not 'who is being difficult' but 'where is the dickhead decision, and what happens to the person who first said we got this wrong.'
points: Claydon's core mechanism — a dickhead decision gets protected rather than revised when reality contradicts it, which then requires a 'behavioural infrastructure' of bullying, coercion, and concealment to sustain — gives leaders a diagnostic for tracing 'toxic culture' back to a specific originating decision rather than treating it as free-floating.

The 'stern ruler to foolish paternalist' framing pinpoints exactly how intelligent, previously successful leaders go wrong: 'their intelligence helped them make sense of the world that produced their success. Dickheadedness begins when they continue imposing that understanding on a world that has moved on.'

His warning about resilience programmes is a genuinely counterintuitive and actionable leadership point: 'teaching people to endure a dickhead system more effectively can increase the durability of the dickhead system' — meaning some wellness interventions treat the wrong patient.

The closing diagnostic question — 'what happens to someone who says, early and clearly, I think we may have got this wrong' — is a concrete, testable measure any leader can apply to their own organization's real psychological safety.
quotes: A dickhead decision gets made. Then people become dicks trying to make reality conform to it.

Some systems can absorb the embarrassment of being wrong. They reconsider assumptions, revise targets, alter course, and learn. Others protect the original decision. That is when an ordinary error starts becoming a dickhead decision.
Their intelligence helped them make sense of the world that produced their success. Dickheadedness begins when they continue imposing that understanding on a world that has moved on.

Those who support it are positive, ambitious, strategic, resilient, commercial. Those who question it are negative, resistant, tactical, cautious, stuck in the past. Evidence has quietly become morality.
Aggression becomes decisiveness. Detachment becomes professionalism. Intimidation becomes accountability. Denial becomes resilience. Manipulation becomes getting things done.
The institution asks people to distrust their own judgment while holding them accountable for demonstrating conviction. Self-betrayal becomes a professional competence.
Teaching people to endure a dickhead system more effectively can increase the durability of the dickhead system.
And perhaps most importantly: What happens to someone who says, early and clearly, "I think we may have got this wrong"?
